content: Hypertension is a significant global public health issue, affecting over one billion individuals worldwide. It disproportionately impacts populations in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), where healthcare systems are often under-resourced. The rising prevalence of hypertension is linked to factors such as population growth, aging, genetic predisposition, and modifiable behavioral risks. These risks include excessive consumption of salt and fat, physical inactivity, obesity, harmful alcohol use, and inadequate stress management. Over time, hypertension contributes to an increased risk of cardiovascular events, including heart disease, stroke, kidney failure, disability, and premature death. Cardiovascular events associated with hypertension are preventable, particularly when high-risk populations are identified and targeted through population-wide screening strategies. In resource-limited settings, a total risk approach—considering multiple risk factors such as age, gender, lifestyle habits, diabetes, and blood cholesterol levels—can improve the precision of identifying high-risk groups. This targeted approach can reduce healthcare costs by focusing resources on those most at risk rather than the entire population. Early detection of hypertension and its associated risk factors through screening can help identify high-risk individuals, enabling timely intervention and management. This can ultimately reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with hypertension. Additionally, early detection can help control healthcare costs by preventing severe complications that may require hospitalization or intensive care due to poorly managed risk factors and comorbidities. The objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of various hypertension screening strategies—mass, targeted, or opportunistic—in reducing hypertension-related morbidity and mortality. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS-Web), CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). The search was unrestricted by language, publication year, or status and included studies up to April 9, 2020. The selection criteria included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized controlled trials (NRCTs), such as controlled before-and-after studies, interrupted time series, and prospective analytic cohort studies. These studies involved healthy adolescents, adults, and elderly individuals participating in mass, targeted, or opportunistic hypertension screening programs. The data collection and analysis process involved screening all retrieved studies using Covidence. Pairs of reviewers independently assessed the titles and abstracts of identified studies and reviewed full texts for potentially eligible studies. Studies were included for full-text screening if two reviewers agreed or if consensus was reached with a third reviewer. The plan was for at least two reviewers to independently extract data, assess the risk of bias using pre-specified Cochrane criteria, and either conduct a meta-analysis of sufficiently similar studies or provide a narrative synthesis of the results. A total of 9,335 titles and abstracts were screened, and 54 studies were identified as potentially eligible for full-text review. However, none of these studies met the eligibility criteria for inclusion in the analysis. The authors concluded that while there is an implicit assumption that early detection of hypertension through screening can reduce morbidity and mortality, this assumption has not been rigorously tested. There is a lack of high-quality evidence from RCTs or programmatic evidence from NRCTs regarding the effectiveness, costs, or potential harms of different hypertension screening strategies—whether mass, targeted, or opportunistic—in reducing hypertension-related morbidity and mortality.
